claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.
Increasing Al content in the multiprincipal-element alloy enhances oxidation resistance by promoting rapid formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale.
Al can be introduced by substituting a controlled fraction of one or more base elements while retaining multiprincipal-element character.
Increased Al preferentially oxidizes during high-temperature exposure to form Al2O3.
The modified alloy develops a continuous, adherent, selective Al2O3 surface scale.
Lattice distortion elevates vacancy formation energy and Al migration barriers.
Lattice distortion suppresses sustained Al diffusion from the substrate or Al-depletion zone.
Suppression of Al diffusion slows oxide-scale growth and spallation during prolonged exposure.
The stable Al2O3 layer limits oxygen ingress and outward metal-cation diffusion.
Limiting oxygen and cation transport preserves bulk material integrity.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, the Al-enhanced alloy will show lower mass gain per unit area under identical oxidation conditions.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, the Al-enhanced alloy will develop a thinner oxide scale.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, the Al-enhanced alloy will exhibit improved scale adhesion and less spallation.
During high-temperature oxidation, equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn forms a multilayer oxide scale.
The equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn baseline has relatively high oxide-growth rates and a tendency toward spallation.
The proposed mechanism should govern behavior from approximately 900°C to 1200°C during prolonged exposure.
Processing history and microstructural variables are to be held constant between baseline and modified alloys.
The quantitative reductions in mass gain and scale-growth rate are uncertain because of competing oxidation pathways and processing-induced microstructural variation.
